newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's top labor leader dies, workers salute him.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's top labor leader dies, workers salute him.

text.p: Mexico's veteran labour leader Fidel Velazquez, who for more than half a century led the country's union movement in unswerving loyalty to a string of presidents, died on Saturday at age 97.
"He died of heart and respiratory failure" in a military hospital, said heart specialist Carlos Castro, Velazquez's son-in-law.

Velazquez, head of the 6 million-strong Mexican Workers Confederation (CTM), was a major national figure and swung worker support behind the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) reliably since 1941.
His death robs the PRI of a key ally less than two weeks before congressional elections, when the party could lose its 68-year-old majority in the lower house.

President Ernesto Zedillo immediately issued a statement mourning Velazquez's death, referring to him affectionately as "Don Fidel" -- the way he was known to nine successive presidents who invariably worked to keep him and his workers on their side.

"Don Fidel dedicated his life to organising workers in demand and defence of their rights. The conquests of Mexican workers ... owe much to the vision and performance of this great leader," the statement said.

In a bid to avoid any damaging succession struggle in the monolithic CTM, his replacement was named immediately. Deputy secretary general Leonardo Rodriguez Alcaine told reporters he would take Velazquez's place until February 1998 when the confederation will hold a new ballot.

At the CTM's headquarters opposite Mexico's giant Monument to the Revolution in the city centre, thousands of workers from some of the 11,000 unions in the CTM cried "Fidel, Fidel" as the casket bearing his embalmed corpse was carried in.

Workers, many dressed in factory overalls, wept openly. As the coffin was opened, cameramen fought for images of the dead leader, and one of Velazquez's sons tried to fight them back with kicks. Zedillo was due to pay his last respects later.
The cigar-chomping former milkman had been in and out of hospital for most of this year, looking increasingly frail, though still influential behind the scenes.
Death cheated him of what he had said was his one remaining goal in life -- to reach his 100th birthday leading the CTM.
Porfirio Munoz Ledo of the leftist Party of the Democratic Revolution described Velazquez's death as a prelude to the death of the PRI in the July 6 elections.
But PRI leader Humberto Roque Villanueva responded icily: "It is not the prelude to anything."

Although Velazquez retained the affection and respect of official labour leaders, he faced increasing challenges in his last years from independently organised unions who wanted to oppose the government.
The CTM's annual May Day parade in central Mexico City with thousands of workers marching under the gaze of the president for decades symbolised the links between organised labour and the government.

But after Mexico plunged into economic crisis in December 1994 and workers' real incomes collapsed, the CTM cancelled its 1995 May Day parade. Fears about the loyalty of union members forced Velazquez to cancel the 1996 and 1997 parades too.
